children: By Janna Herron
One of the biggest retirement worries people have is running out of money.
A widely used score in financial planning tells you the likelihood of that happening.
Advisors often run Monte Carlo simulations to stress-test your retirement savings. The goal is to see if your savings will last your lifetime under a host of different scenarios.
But here's the deal: Most planners don't want you to aim for a 99% or 100% score, because it means you aren't spending enough in retirement. Instead, many planners prefer scores around 85%.
Having a good idea of what the score means, what you should aim for and how to pivot if the score is too low are key to helping you prepare for a smooth retirement.
Let's start at the beginning.
What is the Monte Carlo retirement score?
Nicknamed for the 1863 casino in Monaco, this retirement tool commonly runs a thousand different scenarios to see how your current retirement savings plan performs.
In bad stock markets and in good ones. During high inflation and low inflation. Through long-term care.
The tool uses its own default inputs or ones that you provide. It also factors in your yearly retirement spending goals or the legacy you hope to leave your children.
The tool spits back a percentage. A 65% score means your retirement plan would have roughly a two-thirds chance of succeeding
"It tells you how likely that is to happen and how likely you are to run out of money chasing that goal,"said Jeff Judge, managing partner at Chesapeake Financial Planners.
What should I aim for?
The good news is that your retirement score isn't like a school grade. You don't need to be an A+ retirement saver. In fact, many financial planners want you just above average.

"If someone's got an 85% Monte Carlo, that's great. Eighty-five percent of the time, you're going to be just fine," said Amy Kelly, founder of Kelly Wealth Advisors. "There's 15% where the market returns just don't help you and we got to watch your spending."
For the most part, financial planners use the score to help get your retirement plan on the right trajectory, especially if your score is below the 80s.

Savers, especially those 10 to 15 years from retirement, can employ several levers to increase their score. They can save more. They can work longer. Or they can spend less in retirement, which, Kelly said, "is the biggest driver of what moves the needle."
What happens if the unexpected happens?
Even if your retirement score lands in that targeted mid-80s and above range, one of those 15% scenarios can still happen. You aren't necessarily in trouble.
"There are different ways to course correct," Leyla Morgillo, a financial planner with Madison Financial Planning Group, said.

For example, if the market plunges just when you plan to retire, you may work for another year until it recovers. Perhaps you pick up a part-time job, so you pull less than planned from your portfolio. Or you might tap your home equity instead of selling beaten-down stocks to pay for an unexpected expense.

Kelly looks at her client's budgets to determine how nimble they can be during a down market. Do they have many fixed expenses that never change? Or are they able to make changes in their lifestyle if needed?
"Because that's the name of the game," Kelly said. "You got to have the ability to cut back, so that your portfolio can survive a downturn."
The limitations of the Monte Carlo score
While the Monte Carlo score is useful in getting a bead on your retirement preparedness, it isn't foolproof.
"The biggest weakness is that people can give the output more precision than it deserves," said Scott Bishop, managing director at Presidio Wealth Partners.

The tool is only as good as its inputs-expected returns, volatility, inflation, longevity, spending and correlations-and no one knows what each one will do with certainty. In fact, different planning softwares crank out different scores on the same retirement portfolio because they don't use the same assumptions or methodologies.

Taxes can upend results. Many of the simulations use flat taxes instead of tax brackets, said Bishop, a certified public accountant. That can make a "huge difference" depending on where your money is stored, such as a traditional tax-deferred individual retirement account versus a tax-free Roth IRA versus taxable brokerage accounts.

Those retiring early may want to revisit their Monte Carlo score more often, Morgillo said. More can change over a 50-year retirement horizon than a 25- to 35-year one, especially your planned spending. If you are spending more, "we need to go back and relook at things," she said.
Why not 100%?
That kind of uncertainty may lead some people to score as high as possible, in the high 90s or even 100% if the software allows for a perfect score.
"It tells them that they have a lot of capacity to withstand whatever unexpected thing might pop up," Morgillo said.
Still, a high score is no guarantee.

One of Kelly's clients, a couple with a high Monte Carlo score, bought a second house with a mortgage in California without consulting their advisor, adding another expense to their spending assumptions. Their score dropped.
The couple, who hadn't yet retired, course-corrected. They intend to work a little longer than they originally planned. Their Monte Carlo score is back up.
The lesson? When it comes to spending, Kelly said, "Don't do drastic things."
